title: Definitive acceptance spec for typed-chunk commit semantics and graceful tool-handshake
creator: Aisha Khan
description:
Purpose: This PRD defines unambiguous acceptance criteria for streaming structured output when invoking external tools/functions. It focuses on typed-chunk commit semantics, graceful handshake and fallback modes, error-class taxonomy, resume/repair behavior, and the minimal observability required for safe rollouts.

Context: Multiple customers have reported brittle integrations when a model emits interleaved structured frames and plain text during streaming function calls. Production incidents revealed three failure patterns: partial-frame truncation at network boundaries, duplicate tool invocations due to client retries, and silent schema drift when model outputs stop including required fields. This document stitches together implementable acceptance tests and rollout rules for the runtime, SDKs, and console observability to prevent these classes of outages.

Non-goals: This spec does not define a model training objective or heuristics for content synthesis accuracy. It also does not mandate specific wire protocols beyond the semantic frames defined (implementations may use HTTP chunked, gRPC streaming, or WebSocket).

Constraints: Backwards compatibility is required for hosted API customers; new semantics should be feature-flagged and gateable per-tenant. Runtime must avoid adding >5ms median tail latency for non-invoking calls. The design must be implementable without changes to existing public SDK APIs beyond optional flags and new event hooks.
acceptance_criteria: Typed-chunk handshake: Every streaming session that supports function/tool-calling must begin with a single handshake frame (type=handshake) that includes a schema_version (string), capabilities (list), and a session_nonce. The runtime accepts sessions without handshake but will mark them as ‘handshake-missing’ in telemetry.

Monotonic commit tokens: Each committed structured fragment must include a commit_id (monotonically increasing string or integer) and a stable_fragment_hash. Consumers must be able to identify causal order and detect missing commit_ids. Acceptance test: when server sends commit_id sequence [1,2,4], client flags missing commit_id 3 and logs an event to the console with a severity of WARN or above.

Soft-final and hard-final frames: Streams must support soft-final frames (type=soft_final) that indicate 'likely complete' and hard-final frames (type=final) that indicate guaranteed end-of-output. Clients must treat soft-final as advisory and keep the session open to accept late commits for up to the configured soft_final_grace window (default 500ms). Acceptance test: runtime must allow a late commit with commit_id > last_seen within the grace window and reconcile it into final state without duplicate tool calls.

Idempotent tool invocation: The runtime must attach an idempotency_key derived from session_nonce + target_function_name + commit_id to every tool invocation. On retries, downstream tool gateways should receive identical idempotency_key for the same logical call. Acceptance test: simulate a retry on network disconnect and verify downstream sees a single invocation for the idempotency_key within a 60s window.

Partial-emission reconciliation: When partial JSON fragments are emitted across multiple chunks, the runtime must reconstruct and validate against the advertised schema_version before delivering to the tool layer. Acceptance test: deliver a fragmented object split across 4 chunks; the tool invocation must receive a single, schema-valid payload or the runtime must return a structured parse_error frame with location and expected type hints.

Schema drift detection & fallback: If a committed fragment fails schema validation with a new type for a required field, runtime must emit an explanatory frame (type=schema_violation) with severity and example offending fragment, then automatically fallback to a conservative text-only response mode for that session. Acceptance test: inject schema change and verify fallback mode is activated and surfaced in session telemetry within 1s of detection.

Backpressure & flow-control: Client-visible backpressure frames (type=apply_backpressure, with a target_tokens_per_second and estimated_lag_ms) must be supported. If backpressure persists beyond backpressure_timeout (configurable default 2000ms), runtime must either flush a commit or send a soft_final describing partial state. Acceptance test: induce synthetic load and ensure backpressure frames appear and downstreams receive either commit or soft_final within timeout.

Repair & resume semantics: Streams must support a resume protocol where client supplies last_committed_id and last_seen_fragment_hash. The server will re-emit missing commits or a repair_frame containing a repair_patch. Acceptance test: close a session mid-stream, reconnect with last_committed_id=5, server must resend commits 6..N or send a repair_frame that applies cleanly to the client state.

Observability minimums: Each session must emit structured telemetry: session_nonce, schema_version, commit_id range (first..last), number_of_tool_calls, errors (list of framed error codes), and latency quantiles for commit-to-tool-invocation. Acceptance test: console must display these fields for a selected session and export them to the metrics pipeline as tags.

Graceful downgrade path: If the runtime cannot honor typed-chunks (e.g., due to CPU pressure), it must downgrade to 'envelope-less' streaming but include a final_reconciliation token enabling the client to run local reconciliation heuristics. Acceptance test: simulate CPU-overload and verify downgrade occurs with explicit final_reconciliation token and documented client behavior is followed.

Security and replay protections: idempotency_key and session_nonce must be cryptographically random and logged only as truncated prefixes in customer-facing UIs. Acceptance test: ensure console displays only first 8 chars of session_nonce and raw values are available in audit logs in encrypted form per KMS policy.

End-to-end test coverage: For each acceptance scenario above there must be an automated e2e test running under the nightly sanity pipeline that validates both success and failure modes against a mocked tool endpoint and a flaky network simulator.
tests: Unit tests: chunk framing parser, commit_id monotonic validator, schema validator (positive/negative cases)
Integration: runtime + mock tool gateway verifying idempotency, retries, and single-invocation semantics
E2E: SDK client + runtime + console telemetry pipeline reproducing partial-fragment, resume, and downgrade flows (run nightly)
Load: synthetic sessions with 10k concurrent typed-chunk sessions to validate backpressure and CPU fallback thresholds
notes: Design trade-offs considered: a) mandating handshake reduces compatibility but increases safety; chosen to allow opt-out for older clients. b) commit_id as integer simplifies ordering but string allows opaque ids from downstream gateways; we accept both but require monotonicity. c) soft-final grace chosen conservatively (500ms) to balance latency and late-arrival commits.
